name: Thai
sources: Tingsabadh, M. R. Kalaya & Abramson, Arthur S. (1993). Thai. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 23(1), 24-28.

Abramson, Arthur S. (1962). The Vowels and Tones of Standard Thai: Acoustical Measurements and Experiments. Indiana University Research Center in Anthropology, Folklore and Linguistics, Publication 20.

Abramson, Arthur S. (1979). The coarticulation of tones: an acoustic study of Thai. In Studies in Tai and Mon-Khmer Phonetics and Phonology in Honour of Eugénie J. A. Henderson. Chulalongkorn University Press.
Gandour, Jack, Potisuk, Siripong & Dechongkit, Sumalee (1994). Tonal coarticulation in Thai. Journal of Phonetics 22, 477-492.
Potisuk, Siripong, Gandour, Jack & Harper, Mary P. (1996). Acoustic correlates of stress in Thai. Phonetica 53, 200-220.
Morén, Bruce & Zsiga, Elizabeth (2006). The lexical and post-lexical phonology of Thai tones. Natural Language and Linguistic Theory 24, 113-178.
Zsiga, Elizabeth & Nitisaroj, Rattima (2007). Tone features, tone perception, and peak alignment in Thai. Language and Speech 50, 343-383.
Teeranon, Phanintra (2007). The change of Standard Thai high tone: an acoustic study and a perceptual experiment. SKASE Journal of Theoretical Linguistics 4(3).
Luksaneeyanawin, Sudaporn (1998). Intonation in Thai. In Daniel Hirst & Albert Di Cristo (eds.), Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Abramson, Arthur S. & Ren, Nianqi (1990). Distinctive vowel length: duration vs. spectrum in Thai. Journal of Phonetics 18, 79-92.
Lisker, Leigh & Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20, 384-422.
Grabe, Esther & Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the rhythm class hypothesis. In Laboratory Phonology 7. Mouton de Gruyter.
Iwasaki, Shoichi & Ingkaphirom, Preeya (2005). A Reference Grammar of Thai. Cambridge University Press.
contrasts: three-way laryngeal contrast in labial and alveolar stops: voiced b d, voiceless unaspirated p t, voiceless aspirated pʰ tʰ; two-way in velars (k kʰ) and affricates (tɕ tɕʰ)
vowel length in all nine vowel qualities
five tones in live syllables, three in dead syllables
back unrounded ɯ ɤ against back rounded u o
final nasals m n ŋ, final unreleased stops p t k and glottal stop, final glides j w
allophony: final p t k are unreleased; all written final obstruents are neutralised to them (written s, tɕ, d, tʰ as final are [t̚])
written final l and r are [n]
a glottal stop closes a stressed syllable with a short vowel and no other coda, and begins a syllable written with an initial vowel; it is dropped in unstressed syllables
r is a tap or trill in careful speech and is often replaced by l in casual Bangkok speech; l and r in clusters are often dropped
b and d are fully voiced (long voicing lead), sometimes slightly implosive
tɕ and tɕʰ are alveolo-palatal affricates; tɕʰ is sometimes a fricative
long vowels are shortened in unstressed syllables
the diphthongs ia ɯa ua are long; short versions occur only in a few words
syllable_structure: C(C)V(ː)(C) plus tone; every syllable has an onset (a glottal stop if nothing else)
phonotactics: initial clusters are a stop plus r, l or w: pr pl pʰr pʰl tr kr kl kw kʰr kʰl kʰw (a few more in loanwords)
codas are limited to p t k ʔ m n ŋ j w
dead syllables (ending in p t k or a short vowel with glottal stop) carry only low, high or falling tone: low or high with a short vowel, low or falling with a long vowel
live syllables (ending in a long vowel, nasal or glide) carry any of the five tones

stress.rule: The last syllable of a word or phrase is stressed; syllables before it are unstressed and shortened, above all short open syllables.
stress.cues: duration is the main cue (Potisuk, Gandour & Harper 1996); stressed syllables also have the full tone contour and full vowel quality

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed syllables are shortened, long vowels shorten, short a in linking syllables becomes central and loses its glottal stop and its tone contrast
rhythm.notes: The high vocalic variability also reflects the phonemic vowel length contrast.

length.notes: Long vowels are about twice as long as short vowels (Abramson 1962; Abramson & Ren 1990), with small spectral differences. Final nasals and glides are longer after short vowels.

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; declination and a falling tune, with the last syllable lower; politeness and mood particles (khráp, khâ, ná) close most utterances
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by particles (mǎj, said máj; rɯ̌ɯ, said rɯ́), which carry their own tone; the overall register is higher and declination is reduced, a rising tune in Luksaneeyanawin's terms
intonation.wh_question: question word in place, usually at the end; statement-like tune
intonation.continuation: rising or sustained tune on the last syllable of a non-final phrase, with lengthening
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; tunes change the register and the range of the lexical tones and are most visible on the last, stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Luksaneeyanawin (1998) describes a small set of tunes (fall, rise and convoluted variants) laid over the tones.

inventory.name: mid tone (siang saman, สามัญ)
inventory.description: Mid level, drifting down slightly at the end before a pause (32).

inventory.name: low tone (siang ek, เอก)
inventory.description: Starts just below mid and falls gradually to the bottom of the range.
inventory.phonation: modal, may turn creaky at the end

inventory.name: falling tone (siang tho, โท)
inventory.description: Starts high, rises a little to a peak in the first third of the syllable, then falls steeply to low; also written 41 or 451.
inventory.connected_speech: the fall is cut short in non-final and unstressed syllables, leaving a high tone with a small fall

inventory.name: high tone (siang tri, ตรี)
inventory.description: In present-day Bangkok speech it starts near mid, stays there for the first half of the syllable and rises late to high (334 to 45). Abramson (1962) recorded a high level tone with a small final fall; the change is documented by Teeranon (2007).
inventory.connected_speech: mid-high level with a late rise; the rise is smaller in unstressed syllables
inventory.phonation: modal, sometimes with glottal constriction at the end in citation form

inventory.name: rising tone (siang chattawa, จัตวา)
inventory.description: Starts low-mid, dips to the bottom of the range, then rises steeply to high; also written 24 or 114.
inventory.connected_speech: the rise is cut short in non-final and unstressed syllables, leaving a low or low rising tone
inventory.phonation: modal, may be creaky at the low point
inventory.duration: slightly longer than the other tones

sandhi: no categorical tone sandhi between full syllables

tone neutralisation in unstressed syllables: a short open syllable that is not word-final (a linking syllable, most often with short a) loses its final glottal stop and its tone contrast and is said on a mid level pitch whatever its written tone (sanuk, prathet, sabai)

in unstressed syllables and in fast speech the contour tones are simplified: falling keeps its high start with little fall, rising keeps its low start with little rise; the five tones stay distinct in stressed syllables

tonal coarticulation is gradient: carry-over effects are larger and last through about three quarters of the next syllable, anticipatory effects reach back through about half of the preceding syllable (Gandour, Potisuk & Dechongkit 1994)
some common words are said with a different tone from the written one: the question particle written mǎj is said máj, the pronouns written kʰǎw and tɕʰǎn are said kʰáw and tɕʰán
emphatic reduplication of adjectives puts an extra-high tone on the first copy
tone.neutral_tone: No lexical neutral tone. Unstressed linking syllables (short open syllables before the stressed syllable) are short, lose their glottal stop and take a mid level pitch.
tone.notes: Abramson (1962), citation forms on long vowels: mid is level with a slight final fall; low starts a little below mid and falls slowly; falling starts high, peaks early and drops to the bottom; high starts just above mid and climbs to the top of the range; rising starts low, dips and climbs steeply to the top. Morén & Zsiga (2006) and Zsiga & Nitisaroj (2007) show that in running speech the high tone is a late rise and the falling tone a rise-fall with its peak near the middle of the syllable, and that listeners identify the tones from where the pitch peak or valley falls in the syllable (near the middle or at the end). No absolute F0 values are given here.

phonation: voicing lead in b d, short lag in p t k, long lag in pʰ tʰ kʰ
glottal stop as an onset and as the coda of short stressed open syllables
unreleased final stops with glottal reinforcement
creak may occur at the bottom of the low and rising tones; no phonation contrast

problems: the Thai phoneme table is declared in phsource/phonemes as 'phonemetable th shn' with no file of its own, so Thai uses the Shan table unchanged: six Shan tones (24, 11, 32, 55, 42, 343) instead of the five Thai tones, and no long vowels except a

Thai is not flagged as a tone language in src/libespeak-ng/tr_languages.c (the th case only disables numbers), so CalcPitches_Tone() is not used and tone phonemes do not set pitch levels; pitch comes from the default stress-based intonation

dictsource/th_rules is a letter-by-letter placeholder: each consonant letter gives a consonant, a tone digit fixed by consonant class (3 for mid class, 55 for high class, 2 for low class) and an inherent a; there is no syllable parsing, no live or dead syllable tone rule, no vowel length and no neutralisation of final consonants
the four tone marks (mai ek, mai tho, mai tri, mai chattawa) have no rules, and the tokenizer ends the word at them
several vowel signs are mapped to consonants: sara aa, sara am and sara ii give s, mai han-akat and mai yamok give m; สวัสดี comes out as [sawmsads], มา as [mas], ดี as [ds]
the rules write aspirates as kh, ph, th, ch, which are read as a stop plus h and not as the aspirated phonemes k_h, p_h, t_h of the inherited table
numbers are disabled in tr_languages.c although th_list has the digits, and there is no word segmentation for unspaced Thai text
the result is not intelligible as Thai
good: nothing that matters yet: the voice is a placeholder with 'status testing'

notes: The tone field espeak is left empty because eSpeak NG has no Thai tone phonemes. If the inherited Shan tone phonemes had to be used, the nearest matches would be: Thai rising - Shan 1 (24), Thai low - Shan 2 (11), Thai high - Shan 4 (55), Thai falling - Shan 5 (42), Thai mid - Shan 3 (32); none of them is a good match for the Thai contours.
